1) Answer

Strict “proof” of a person’s values is impossible; what we can do is weigh public commitments, policies, and actions while also noting counter-evidence. On balance, multiple primary and high‑quality sources show Mark Rutte repeatedly tying his leadership (as Dutch prime minister and now NATO secretary general) to the protection of human rights, the rule of law, and accountability.

Evidence that Rutte values human rights
- Clear public commitments in multilateral forums:
  - UN General Assembly speeches in 2022 and 2023 where he condemned human rights violations in Russia’s war on Ukraine, called for accountability, and framed Dutch policy around “peace, freedom, [and] justice.” He referenced visiting Bucha and insisted such crimes “must not go unpunished.” ([netherlandsandyou.nl](https://www.netherlandsandyou.nl/web/pr-un-new-york/documents/speeches/2022/09/29?utm_source=openai))
  - Statement at the 2023 Council of Europe summit explicitly defending “freedom, democracy, human rights and the rule of law,” urging action where media freedom, gender equality and LGBTIQ rights are under pressure. ([government.nl](https://www.government.nl/documents/speeches/2023/05/17/statement-by-prime-minister-mark-rutte-at-the-general-debate-of-the-fourth-council-of-europe-summit?utm_source=openai))

- Policies and instruments advanced under his premiership:
  - The Netherlands’ long‑standing human‑rights foreign‑policy priorities (freedom of expression, religion/belief, equal rights for women/girls and LGBTIQ+ people, and protection of human‑rights defenders) and funding lines such as the Human Rights Fund and Human Rights Tulip prize, which his governments maintained and used. ([government.nl](https://www.government.nl/topics/human-rights/human-rights-worldwide?utm_source=openai))
  - The 2022–2026 National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights adopted during his tenure. ([government.nl](https://www.government.nl/topics/responsible-business-conduct-rbc/national-action-plan-on-business-and-human-rights?utm_source=openai))
  - EU-level “Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime” (“EU Magnitsky”), created in 2020 and repeatedly renewed while he was PM, which the Netherlands supported as an EU member state. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2020/12/07/eu-adopts-a-global-human-rights-sanctions-regime/?utm_source=openai))

- Accountability for international crimes:
  - Rutte stressed accountability for atrocities in Ukraine, hosted the Ukraine Accountability Conference in The Hague, and said the Netherlands would support investigations and evidence work with the ICC. ([netherlandsandyou.nl](https://www.netherlandsandyou.nl/web/pr-un-new-york/documents/speeches/2022/09/29?utm_source=openai))
  - He publicly vowed to continue holding Russia to account for MH17. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2023/02/09/ukraine-crisis-mh17-rutte?utm_source=openai))

- Acknowledgement of historical injustice:
  - On 19 Dec 2022 Rutte formally apologized for the Dutch state’s role in slavery, calling it a “crime against humanity,” and his cabinet established a €200 million fund for education and commemoration—concrete policy tied to human dignity. ([government.nl](https://www.government.nl/latest/news/2022/12/19/government-apologises-for-the-netherlands-role-in-the-history-of-slavery?utm_source=openai))

- Upholding rule‑of‑law constraints in sensitive cases:
  - When a Dutch appeals court ordered a halt to exports of F‑35 parts to Israel over risks of IHL violations, the government complied with the order while appealing—illustrating deference to judicial human‑rights scrutiny. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/b33608b054a33fbacc518395b53b74e8?utm_source=openai))

- NATO role and stated values:
  - As NATO Secretary General (since 1 Oct 2024), Rutte leads an alliance whose founding treaty and current declarations bind members to democracy, individual liberty, human rights, and the rule of law; his 2025 appearances emphasized defending these values in practice. ([nato.int](https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/who_is_who_229125.htm?utm_source=openai))

Relevant counter‑evidence (to weigh fairly)
- Domestic rights failure: the childcare benefits scandal (racial/ethnic profiling and due‑process failures) harmed thousands of families and led Rutte III to resign in Jan 2021—serious rule‑of‑law concerns. The government accepted political responsibility and initiated compensation, but the episode weighs against the claim. ([cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/01/15/dutch-government-resigns-after-childcare-benefits-scandal-.html?utm_source=openai))
- Asylum policy controversy: his coalition collapsed in July 2023 after he pushed restrictions including limiting or delaying family reunification for asylum seekers—measures critics argued conflicted with human‑rights and refugee‑protection norms. ([dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/netherlands-government-to-resign-amid-asylum-row/a-66162248?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line
- Rutte’s record contains blemishes—most notably the childcare scandal and restrictive migration proposals. Yet across more than a decade as PM and now at NATO, he has consistently articulated human‑rights principles, maintained concrete Dutch programs that fund and protect human‑rights work, backed EU and international accountability tools, and took high‑salience steps such as the slavery apology and ICC/Ukraine accountability support. That body of evidence is consistent with valuing human rights, while recognizing a mixed domestic record that reasonable observers may weigh differently. ([government.nl](https://www.government.nl/topics/human-rights/human-rights-worldwide?utm_source=openai))
